text:
A data model is only a drawing until code loads it, and that code is usually Python. Say the input is a fifty gigabyte log, and the machine has eight gigabytes of memory. Read the whole file first, and it can't fit. Read it one line at a time, and memory only ever holds a line. That's what the Python round checks: code that moves data without running out of memory, and is safe to run twice. Eighteen questions: fourteen worked through, each run in Python, then four quickly. It starts with one choice: a list, or a generator.

Question one. Why prefer a generator over a list when processing large data? A list holds every element at once. A generator yields one at a time, on demand. The page's parser reads a line, splits it, and yields a name and a quantity. On a file of a million orders, collecting the rows in a list peaks at sixty-three megabytes. Summing straight from the generator peaks at about a hundred fifty kilobytes. Cut the file to a tenth, and so does the list. The generator doesn't move: its memory doesn't depend on the input. Question two. How do generator pipelines compare to building intermediate lists? Here's a three-stage pipeline, twice. With square brackets, each stage is a list, and all three are alive at once: a hundred sixty megabytes. With round brackets, each is a generator, and one row passes through all three before the next is read. Lists still earn their place: you can print one to debug it, and read it twice. A generator is spent after one pass; sum it again, and you get zero. Lists for small data you rescan, generators for large or endless data. Which is how you read a file.
